newsitem.title: USA: US transmission users slam grid access info system.
newsitem.headline: US transmission users slam grid access info system.

text.p: U.S. power producers, traders and marketers Friday slammed the information system the industry designed to provide equal access to utilities' transmission lines and promote bulk power market competition.

The Federal Energy Regulatory commission last year ordered utilities to set up the open access same-time information system, dubbed OASIS, in its rules requiring them to offer all power producers equal service on their transmission lines.

Critics ranted to commission staff Friday that the system, which started up last January, was complex and cumbersome and made it difficult to track and reserve available transmission capacity on the grid.
"It's too slow to support a competitive marketplace," Brian Tierney of Enron Power Marketing, Inc, said at a FERC conference to evaluate the progress of OASIS.
"Our experience with the OASIS has not been a good one so far," said Terry Callender of Electric Clearinghouse, Inc. "We came for a cool drink of water and got a mouthful of hot sand."

The Internet-based system was meant to be a seamless nationwide reservation system, with 22 regional "nodes" for utilities to post available transmission capacity, other services, transfer capability and network reservations, to support bulk power sales.
But instead, users said many utilities were using the system to their own advantage.

"We are concerned about the volume of reservation activity that may still be taking place off OASIS," said Gerry Cauley, who represented the How Working Group, the industry group in charge of designing the system.

Echoing several other companies, Callender said transmission providers posted "incorrect or stale information" on their Internet sites, caused confusion by using different names for the same products and transmission paths, and withheld information on transmission capacity.
"Very little firm ATC (available transmission capacity) is offered, due to caution or strategy," he said.
In some cases, transmission users ran into unhelpful utility staff who knew little about OASIS, or had requests go on hold for days when an OASIS site was unmanned.
"More salmon survive the upstream migration than transmission requests survive on the OASIS," Marjorie Philips of PECO Energy's Power Team.

The companies said the commission should close loopholes in its regulations to ensure that utilities posted all over their available transmission service on their OASIS sites, and clarify how much firm capacity could be held by a utility for its native load.
